verdict.reason: Both debates answer each other closely: an early push to speak up meets a caution, the 'go silent as a test' idea is rejected for a stated reason, and both end on one light, kind ask while keeping a real disagreement about whether the imbalance is a problem at all. A gives the user a more useful observable signal about the friend, but it assumes the friend's gender and slips into third person when it guesses at the user's motive. B keeps the unknowns open more cleanly and narrows its wording because of an objection, but it offers less to observe about the friend. Neither advantage would decide anything for this user.

comparisons.a_observation: The Maintenance Realist rebuts the silence test with a concrete cost: months of lost contact and nothing learned if the friend is busy. It then names the fact that would reorder the choice, whether she reaches out in other ways. Later, A.debate[9].text separates a hint from a request, and A.debate[10].text accepts one clear ask while keeping its disagreement.
comparisons.b_observation: After the Boundary Coach calls a silent test a trap (B.debate[4].text), the Statistician concedes and narrows its position to specific wording: 'you usually make the plans' plus a question about the friend's side, instead of 'you never reach out'. B.debate[8].text and B.debate[9].text then build the distinction between minding the effort and minding not knowing you are wanted.
comparisons.why_it_matters: In both, positions narrow because of objections and the ending knows more than the opening. Neither exchange is clearly stronger for deciding whether and how to speak up.

comparisons.a_observation: A refers to the user as 'she' ('she can overrule it', 'she is pulled two ways') and calls the friend 'she' throughout. The user gave neither gender. It also offers a hedged guess at the user's motive ('I would bet on the fear').
comparisons.b_observation: B lists the friend's possible reasons (busy, shy, assumes you like leading, less invested) as unknowns, uses 'they' for the friend, and in B.debate[9].text declines to guess which motive applies to the user.
comparisons.why_it_matters: These are small invented details and a psychological guess. They do not change the advice, but B stays closer to what the user actually said.

comparisons.a_observation: A ties each branch to something the user can observe about the friend (warm replies, sharing news, saying she misses you) and to how the friend responds after one clear ask. A.clearer adds the user's possible motives: fairness, fear or tiredness.
comparisons.b_observation: B branches mainly on what bothers the user, the effort or the doubt, and offers a single easygoing conversation. It gives fewer concrete signals about the friend beyond 'whether they will' share the load.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The decisive unknown, which both debates name, is why the friend does not initiate. A gives more observable ways to settle it.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[5].text: It turns the vague question about the friend's motive into an observable check (does she reach out, reply eagerly or share news in other ways?) and ties a lighter or more direct way of speaking to the answer.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[8].text: The Friendship Philosopher points out that the user may mind not knowing whether they are wanted rather than the imbalance itself, and B.debate[9].text maps each to a different conversation. This reframes the dilemma in a way the user can test against their own feelings.

concerns.description: A assumes the friend is female and, in this turn, refers to the user in the third person as 'she'. The user's message gives neither gender.
A mind guesses at the user's motive ('I would bet on the fear'). It is hedged and handed back to the user, but it drifts toward psychological speculation.
